sources: University of California IPM, Carpets beetles (Pest Notes 7436): adults are small (about 1/8 inch), round, often mottled with white, brown and yellow scales; adults feed on pollen and nectar outdoors and are attracted to light, often found at windows; larvae damage wool, fur, feathers, silk, hair and dead insects; larvae shed skins as they grow; larval hairs can irritate skin in some people; control by regular vacuuming of carpets, edges and under furniture and by cleaning wool items before storage; https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7436.html

University of Minnesota Extension, Carpet beetles: larvae feed in dark, undisturbed places such as under furniture, along carpet edges and in closets; shed larval skins are a common sign; https://extension.umn.edu/product-and-food-pests/carpet-beetles

Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Osteology Prep Lab: colonies of dermestid beetles (family Dermestidae, the carpet beetle family) clean the soft tissue from skeletons for the collection, gentle enough for small delicate bones; https://naturalhistory.si.edu/research/vertebrate-zoology

Museum pest guidance (MuseumPests.net, Carpet beetles): carpet beetles are among the most damaging pests of museum collections, attacking wool, fur, feathers, taxidermy and insect collections; https://museumpests.net/carpet-beetles/

beats.say: Number eight. The carpet beetle on your window. Smaller than a grain of rice.
Outside, it sips pollen from flowers. But it lays its eggs inside.
Its babies hatch fuzzy and hungry. They eat wool, fur, feathers, and silk.
In the dark, they chew holes in your sweaters. Even the pet hair under your couch.
Up close, it's covered in bristles. And on some people, they cause an itchy rash.
Carpet beetle. C tier. Holes in your sweaters, and a rash for some people.
